title: Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus
goal: By the end you can build four small designs that use the whole track: an `Either<out L, out R>` that leans on `Nothing`, a storeroom with a covariant display-case view, a typed board of delivery bells that stores listeners behind adapters, and a container of typed keys that carry a `KType`. For each type parameter, you can say why it is `out`, `in` or invariant.
opening:
Picture the back door of the fruit shop on a busy day. Deliveries arrive from morning to night, and a board of bells hangs by the door, one bell for each kind of delivery. When apples arrive, the apple bell rings, and everyone who asked to hear it comes: the sign-writer, who writes a card for each variety, and the stock-keeper, who counts every fruit of any kind.

Wiring up that board is where people slip. The board keeps one list of listeners per bell, and every list must accept any fruit. The sign-writer only understands apples. Force the sign-writer onto that list with a cast, and it compiles. It even works, until the day a lemon reaches the sign-writer.

Advanced generics: recursive bounds, T & Any, @UnsafeVariance ended with that question, and this last lesson of the track answers it with everything since lesson 1. In this lesson, we'll build four small designs: a result that is either a problem or a fruit, a storeroom with a read-only display case, the board of bells, and a container whose keys carry their value's type. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: `sealed interface Either<out L, out R>` with `data class Left<out L>(val value: L) : Either<L, Nothing>`. In `fun <L, R, R2> Either<L, R>.map(f: (R) -> R2): Either<L, R2>`, can the `Left` branch simply return `this`?
options: No: `this` is an `Either<L, R>`, and the function must return an `Either<L, R2>`
Yes: a `Left<L>` is an `Either<L, Nothing>`, which is an `Either<L, R2>` because `Nothing` is a subtype of `R2` and `R` is `out`
Only with an unchecked cast to `Either<L, R2>`
Only if `R2` is the same type as `R`
warmup.why: After the smart cast, `this` is a `Left<L>`, whose declared supertype is `Either<L, Nothing>`. With `out R`, `Nothing` below `R2` means `Either<L, Nothing>` is below `Either<L, R2>`. So one `Left` object is a valid result for any success type. Java, with no `Nothing`, has to build a new `Left` in that branch.

compare.title: The board of bells in Java and Kotlin

java.title: BellBoard.java

kotlin.title: BellBoard.kt

compare.note: The design is the same in both languages: keys from the item's run-time class, listeners stored behind an adapter that checks the class and casts, and a listener parameter that accepts supertypes. Where Java writes the variance at each use (`Class<? extends Fruit>` keys, `Consumer<? super E>` listeners), Kotlin gets it from declarations: `item::class` is already a `KClass<out Fruit>`, and a function type is already `in` on its parameter, so `(E) -> Unit` needs no projection. Kotlin also adds the reified wrapper, which needs `noinline` because the lambda is stored. Java callers can reach the `KClass` version only through `JvmClassMappingKt.getKotlinClass(Apple.class)`, so a board meant for Java code should also offer a `Class<E>` overload.

worked.title: Receive a delivery note through all four designs

steps.say: A delivery note arrives as a map of text fields, read from a paper form. 1. Parse it into an `Either` instead of throwing, so the caller decides what a bad note means.

2. Ring the bell for each good delivery. 3. Record each problem in the day's typed attributes. Self-check before reading the comment: why can `Either.Right(Apple(name, grams))` be returned where `Either<String, Fruit>` is expected? (`Right<Apple>` is an `Either<Nothing, Apple>`, and both parameters are `out`.)

4. Wire the listeners once, when the shop opens. The stock-keeper is a `(Fruit) -> Unit` and listens under both kinds; the sign-writer only understands apples. A nightly report lists the suppliers through the covariant `DisplayCase<Item<*>>`. Every type parameter in this flow has the variance its role demands, and the only casts are the two that are safe by construction: `safeCast` in the board's adapter, and the unchecked cast inside `Attributes.get`.

lab.title: Build Either, a storeroom, a board of bells and typed keys
steps: Run the tests. All thirteen fail. Work through the files in order; each part has its own tests.
`Either.kt` (a TODO in each of two functions): write `map` with `is Either.Left -> this`, and `getOrElse`.
`Storeroom.kt` (TODOs 1 to 3): add `out` to `DisplayCase`. Back `InMemoryStoreroom` with a `java.util.TreeMap<ID, T>`. Write `saveAll` and `describeAll`.

`BellBoard.kt` (TODOs 4 to 6): store an adapter in `listen`, make the one-argument `listen` inline with a `reified E` and a `noinline` listener, and write `ring` so it returns the number of listeners that ran.

`Attributes.kt` (TODOs 7 and 8): make `key` inline and reified with `typeOf<T>()`, then write `set`, `get`, `getOrDefault` and `remove`. Use `key in values` for `getOrDefault`, so a stored `null` is not mistaken for a missing key.
Run until all thirteen pass. Then remove `out` from `DisplayCase` once more and watch which test turns red.
hints: A `TreeMap` works as `byId[item.id] = item`, and `byId.values.toList()` is already in id order.
The adapter is `bells.getOrPut(type) { mutableListOf() }.add { item -> type.safeCast(item)?.let(listener) }`. `safeCast` needs `import kotlin.reflect.safeCast`.
`ring`: `val listeners = bells[item::class] ?: return 0`, then call each one and return `listeners.size`.
Each unchecked cast in `Attributes` needs `@Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")`. Write one comment that says why it's safe: only `set(key: Key<T>, value: T)` puts values in, and `Key` is invariant.

drill.title: Write Either and map from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write `Either` with `Left` and `Right` in Kotlin, with the variance and the `Nothing` that let `map` return `this` for a `Left`. Write `map`. Then write the Java version with a sealed interface and records, and point at the line where Java has to build a new object.

alt.title: Either.java

recap: `Either<out L, out R>` with `Left : Either<L, Nothing>` lets one `Left` stand for every success type, so `map` can return `this`. Java must rebuild it.
When a type both reads and writes `T`, give the reading half its own `out T` interface, the display case. Readers get covariance; the full storeroom stays invariant and safe.

On a board of bells, deliveries are produced and listeners consume. Keys are `KClass<out Fruit>` from `item::class`, listeners sit behind a `safeCast` adapter rather than a cast, and a reified wrapper that stores its lambda needs `noinline`.
A typed key carries its value's type (`Key<T>` with a `KType` inside), so reads need no cast and same-named keys of different types don't collide.
A key is used to write, so it must be invariant. With `out T`, a wrong value goes in and fails later as a `ClassCastException`.
The limit: these designs check types, not meaning, and the board rings only for the exact class. When a design needs much more, a sealed class and a `when` are often plainer.
closing:
We started at the back door, with a board of bells and a sign-writer who only understands apples. From lesson 1's labeled box on, the whole track went into four designs: an `Either` whose `Left` fits every success type, a display case that lets readers in and keeps writers out, a board that keeps narrow listeners behind a checking adapter, and keys that carry their value's type and stay invariant.

Search your code for `@Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")`. Each one should sit somewhere private, with a comment that says why it's safe by construction.

Next, we'll start a new track, Functional programming in Kotlin, with pure functions, the idea everything else builds on. How can a function have more inputs than parameters?

quiz.q: Which interface can safely be declared with `out T`?
options: `interface Storeroom<T> { fun save(item: T): T }`
`interface Slot<T> { var current: T }`
`interface DisplayCase<T> { fun findAll(): List<T> }`
`interface Key<T> { val name: String }`, used as `set(key: Key<T>, value: T)`
quiz.why: `DisplayCase` only hands `T` out. `save` takes a `T`, and a `var` is both read and written, so those must be invariant. The key is the subtle one: it has no `T` member at all, so `out T` would compile, but it is used to choose what may be written, and `out` would let `set(key, 42)` through.

quiz.q: On the board of bells, why can't `listen` simply do `bells[type]!!.add(listener)` with `listener: (E) -> Unit` and a list of `(Fruit) -> Unit`?
options: Because lambdas can't be stored in a map
Because `(E) -> Unit` is not a `(Fruit) -> Unit`: function parameters are `in`, and a listener for apples can't take a lemon
Because `E` is erased, so the list can't hold it
It can; the adapter is only there for speed
quiz.why: A `(Fruit) -> Unit` must accept every fruit. A listener that only takes `Apple` doesn't, so the compiler refuses the `add`. The adapter takes any fruit and passes on only those that `safeCast` to `E`. The other direction works: a `(Fruit) -> Unit` listener is an `(Apple) -> Unit`.

quiz.q: Why does the reified `listen` need `noinline` on its listener parameter?
options: Because reified functions can't take lambdas
Because Java callers need it
Because the listener is stored in the map, so it must exist as an object instead of being inlined
Because `noinline` makes the type parameter reified
quiz.why: Lambdas passed to an inline function are inlined too, so they don't exist as values. A lambda you store, return or pass on to a function that isn't inline must stay an object, which `noinline` asks for. It has nothing to do with `reified`, which is about the type parameter.

quiz.q: `data class Key<T>(val name: String, val type: KType)`. Why include the `KType` when the key already has a name?
options: So that `key<List<Int>>("weights")` and `key<Int>("weights")` are different keys and can't collide
Because a data class needs at least two properties
So that `get` can cast without an unchecked warning
Because a `KType` makes the key covariant
quiz.why: With the name alone, two keys with the same name and different value types would share one slot, and reading one would return the other's value. The `KType` from `typeOf<T>()` makes them unequal. The cast in `get` is still unchecked; it is safe because only `set` puts values in.

quiz.q: From "Star projection: when you don't know the type": a helper reports the size of any in-memory list, a `MutableList<Apple>`, a `MutableList<String>` or anything else, and may clear it. Which parameter type fits best?
options: `MutableList<Any?>`
`MutableList<in Any>`
`MutableList<Fruit>`
`MutableList<*>`
quiz.why: The helper neither reads typed elements nor writes any, so a star projection says exactly that and accepts every mutable list, while still allowing `size` and `clear()`. `MutableList<Any?>` accepts only lists whose element type is exactly `Any?`, and `in Any` accepts only lists of `Any` or `Any?`. `MutableList<Fruit>` turns away both the apple list and the string list.

flashcards.front: Why is `Left` declared `Left<out L>(val value: L) : Either<L, Nothing>`?
flashcards.back: So one `Left` fits `Either<L, R>` for every `R`: `Nothing` is a subtype of every type, and `Either` is `out` in `R`.

flashcards.front: A storeroom both saves and returns `T`. How do you let read-only code accept a storeroom of any item?
flashcards.back: Split out `interface DisplayCase<out T> { fun findAll(): List<T> }` and have the full `Storeroom` extend it. Readers take `DisplayCase<Item<*>>`.

flashcards.front: What type do the keys of a class-keyed board of bells have, and why?
flashcards.back: `KClass<out Fruit>`, because `item::class` on a `Fruit` has exactly that type.

flashcards.front: How do you store an `(Apple) -> Unit` in a list of `(Fruit) -> Unit`?
flashcards.back: Wrap it: `{ item -> Apple::class.safeCast(item)?.let(listener) }`. The adapter takes any fruit and passes on only an `Apple`.

flashcards.front: When does a lambda parameter of an inline function need `noinline`?
flashcards.back: When the function stores it, returns it or passes it to code that isn't inline, as `listen` does with its map of listeners.

flashcards.front: Why must a typed `Key<T>` be invariant?
flashcards.back: It decides what may be written. With `out T`, a `Key<List<String>>` could act as a `Key<Any>`, `set(key, 42)` would compile, and the next read would throw `ClassCastException`.

terms.plain: A result that is a problem (`Left`) or a value (`Right`), declared `out` in both.
Splitting a type's reading half into its own covariant interface, so readers get flexibility the full type can't have.
An object that passes each event, a message that something happened, to everyone who asked for that kind of event.
A small wrapper that turns one function type into another, here by checking the item's class first.
Marks a lambda parameter of an inline function that must stay an object, because it is stored.
A key object that carries the type of its value, so a container can return that type without casts.
An unchecked cast that can't fail, because a private rule guarantees what was stored.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate reviews the lab's `BellBoard` and asks two things: why the board wraps every listener in a lambda instead of storing it directly, and why the stock-keeper, typed `(Fruit) -> Unit`, can listen under `Apple::class`. Explain both with the producer and consumer picture.
explain_back.answer: Deliveries are produced at the back door and consumed by listeners, so a listener's type is `in` on its parameter. That gives both answers. A listener typed `(Apple) -> Unit` can only consume apples, so it is not a `(Fruit) -> Unit`, which must consume any fruit. The board keeps one list of `(Fruit) -> Unit` per class, so it can't store the apple listener as it is. It stores an adapter instead: a function that takes any `Fruit`, checks it with `Apple::class.safeCast`, and passes it on only if it really is an apple. Casting the listener would compile, but it would fail with a `ClassCastException` inside the listener the first time a lemon arrived. The stock-keeper goes the other way. It consumes every `Fruit`, so it can certainly consume apples. Because the parameter is `in`, a `(Fruit) -> Unit` is an `(Apple) -> Unit`, and `listen(Apple::class, stockCount)` type-checks with `E = Apple`.

deeper.body:
Each design has a natural next step.

The board rings only for the item's exact class. To ring a listener under `Fruit::class` for an apple too, `ring` must walk the item's supertypes. Without kotlin-reflect you can do that through Java reflection: `item.javaClass.interfaces` and `item.javaClass.superclass`, converted with `.kotlin`. With kotlin-reflect, `KClass.allSuperclasses` lists them directly. Cache the result per class, since the walk is the same every time.

`Either` gets more useful with `flatMap`, which chains steps that can each fail: `fun <L, R, R2> Either<L, R>.flatMap(f: (R) -> Either<L, R2>): Either<L, R2>`. Its `Left` branch returns `this` for the same reason `map` can. The standard library's own `Result<out T>` is declared `out` too, but its failure side is always a `Throwable`; `Either` lets the problem be a type of your own, such as a `DeliveryProblem`. Libraries such as Arrow ship a full `Either`.

The storeroom can grow a write-only view as well: `interface Intake<in T> { fun save(item: T) }`. A loader that writes `Supplier`s can then accept an `Intake<Item<Long>>`. With both views, the invariant `Storeroom` is simply the type that is both.

The typed keys can carry a default: `class Key<T>(val name: String, val type: KType, val default: T)`, with `get` returning `T` instead of `T?`. Keep `Key` invariant when you do: `default` is read, but `set` still writes through the key.
